title: Thank your body
hookLine: this body carried you all the way here

lines: A HEART, A PAIR OF HANDS.
cards: A heart keeps time through arguments, weddings and bad nights, without once asking to be noticed. Hands learn to hold a spoon, then a pen, then someone else's hand.
A person can spend years criticizing a body and never once thank it. This block of the path has been about endings, and the body is the part of us that will one day end.
Today: a psalm, a bathroom blessing and a letter of Paul's, each thanking it while it's still here.

teach.b: In Psalm one hundred thirty-nine, the psalmist speaks to God about being formed before birth, and then says: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works."
It isn't praise for a perfect body. It's praise for a made one, a body someone took care over.
Second, a blessing for openings. Jewish tradition has a blessing called Asher Yatzar, said after using the bathroom.

In paraphrase, it blesses God who formed the human body with wisdom, with openings and hollows, and notes that if one of them were blocked or opened when it shouldn't be, a person couldn't stand and live.
It's a thank-you for plumbing, said again and again through the day, and honest about how fragile the whole thing is.

teach.h: NO PART CAN SAY NO NEED.
teach.b: Third, no part can say no need.

In his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul uses the body as a picture of a community: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you."
He's talking about people in a church, but the picture works because it's true of bodies first.
Gratitude for a body doesn't have to wait until it's well or young or the shape you'd like. A body that's tired, sore, scarred or ill has still carried you here. It can be thanked exactly as it is.

how: Observant Jews say the Asher Yatzar blessing after using the bathroom, thanking God for the body's workings; some people of other paths practice a slow body scan with thanks, part by part.

o: a Jewish blessing thanking God for the body's design
a Jewish greeting said when meeting an old friend
a Hebrew psalm sung at the start of Shabbat

games.q: what's inside today's thanks — tap the pairs.
p: a blessing for the body's openings
the eye cannot say to the hand
thanks for the body as it is

s: the psalm praises a perfect body
it praises a made one: I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Asher Yatzar is said after using the bathroom
it thanks God for the body's openings and hollows.
in Paul's picture the head can do without the feet
nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.

games.q: a part of your body hurts, and it's hard to thank. what does today's practice suggest?
o: force yourself to feel grateful for it.
simply notice it, and move on.
games.why: the practice says you can simply notice a hard part and move on; a body that's sore still carried you here.

practice: Starting at your feet, move slowly upward, silently thanking each part: your legs for every step, your belly for digesting, your chest and lungs for this breath, your heart for keeping time, your hands and shoulders for carrying so much, then your face, your eyes, your ears.
If a part hurts or is hard to thank, simply notice it and move on. If you pray, you can turn the thanks toward God.

wordCard.voice: Asher Yatzar, the Jewish blessing thanking God who formed the body with wisdom, openings and all. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: who formed. the opening words, after the blessing formula, of the Jewish blessing for the body.

carryVoice: Your line: thank you, body. Tired or well, it has carried you this far. Go gently.
